q: What are the four attribute types?
short: Nominal (labels), ordinal (ordered labels), interval (meaningful differences, arbitrary zero), ratio (true zero, meaningful ratios).
detail: Each supports more operations: nominal =, ≠; ordinal <, >; interval +, −; ratio ×, ÷. The type decides valid statistics and encodings.
mistakes: Treating zip codes as numbers to average.

q: Discrete vs continuous attributes?
short: Discrete take countable values (counts, codes); continuous take real values (height, temperature).
detail: Binary is a special case of discrete. Continuous values are stored with finite precision as floats.
example: Number of visits vs spend amount.
follow: Can a discrete attribute be ratio-scaled?
mistakes: Equating discrete with categorical.

q: Name common data quality problems.
short: Noise, outliers, wrong or fake data, missing values, duplicates, inconsistencies.
detail: Quality dimensions: correct, complete, consistent, trustworthy, interpretable, available on demand.
example: Salary −10, Age 42 with birth year 2010, 1 Jan as default birthday.
follow: How would you detect disguised missing values?
mistakes: Assuming nulls are the only missing values.

q: Noise vs outliers?
short: Noise is random distortion of values; outliers are objects very different from the rest, which may be errors or the very thing you want to find.
detail: Noise usually needs smoothing or robust models; outliers need investigation: remove, cap or model them.
example: Static on a call vs a fraudulent transaction.
mistakes: Deleting all outliers blindly.

q: How do you handle missing values?
short: Drop rows/columns with too many gaps, or impute: constant, last value, mean/median/mode, interpolation, or a model; optionally add a missing-indicator.
detail: Choice depends on the missingness mechanism and data type; time series prefer forward-fill or interpolation; mean imputation shrinks variance.
example: Monthly air traffic gaps filled by interpolation.
mistakes: Imputing with statistics computed on the full dataset.

q: What is the IQR outlier rule?
short: Flag values below Q1 − 1.5·IQR or above Q3 + 1.5·IQR, where IQR = Q3 − Q1.
detail: Robust because quartiles ignore extremes. Example Q1 = 10, Q3 = 20 gives fences −5 and 35.
mistakes: Using mean ± 1.5·SD and calling it IQR.

q: Normalisation vs standardisation?
short: Normalisation maps values to a fixed range (min-max); standardisation subtracts the mean and divides by the SD.
detail: Normalisation suits bounded, roughly uniform data and distance/NN models; standardisation suits Gaussian-assuming models and is less affected by outliers.
mistakes: Fitting the scaler on the whole dataset.

q: Why use stratified sampling?
short: To keep class (or group) proportions the same in each split, reducing variance and bias of evaluation.
detail: Random splits of small data can distort proportions, e.g. Iris test set 12/22/16 instead of 17/17/16.
mistakes: Stratifying on a feature instead of the target when evaluation needs the target ratio.

q: One-hot vs label encoding?
short: One-hot creates a binary column per category; label encoding maps categories to integers.
detail: Label encoding implies an order: fine for ordinal features or trees, misleading for linear/distance models on nominal data. One-hot can explode with many categories.
example: Fuel Gas/Diesel as two dummy columns.
mistakes: Encoding before cleaning 'Gas' vs 'gas'.

q: What is feature engineering?
short: Creating, selecting and transforming features so the model can learn: extraction, selection, construction, transformation.
detail: Examples: PCA (extraction), dropping redundant columns (selection), customer lifetime from dates (construction), binning and encoding (transformation).
follow: Give an example of feature crossing.
mistakes: Adding features without checking for leakage.

q: A column has 'Gas', 'Diesel' and 'gas'. What happens if you label-encode it directly?
short: You get three codes (1, 2, 3); 'gas' becomes a fake third category.
detail: Normalise case, strip whitespace and map synonyms first; then encode. Also validate unseen categories in production.
follow: How would you detect such issues automatically?
mistakes: Fixing it only in the training data.

q: Compute min-max and z-score for 73,600 with range 12,000–98,000, μ = 54,000, σ = 16,000.
mistakes: Using test-set min/max.

q: Why is the 3-sigma rule less reliable than IQR on small or skewed data?
short: The mean and SD are themselves pulled by outliers (masking), and the 99.7% coverage assumes normality.
detail: IQR uses quartiles, which have a 25% breakdown point. Robust z-scores use median and MAD.
example: One huge value inflates σ and hides itself.
mistakes: Quoting 99% instead of 99.7%.

q: Fraud is 0.3% of your data. How do you train and evaluate?
short: Stratified split; rebalance the training set (under/over-sampling, SMOTE or class weights); evaluate on the untouched test distribution with precision, recall, PR-AUC.
detail: Never rebalance the test set. Tune the threshold for business cost.
mistakes: Over-sampling before splitting.

q: Equal-width vs equal-frequency binning?
short: Equal-width uses fixed-size intervals (W = (B − A)/N); equal-frequency puts about the same count in each bin.
detail: Equal-width is simple but outliers stretch the range and skewed data piles into few bins; equal-frequency adapts to the distribution.
mistakes: Computing bin edges on test data.

q: What is the curse of dimensionality?
short: As features grow, data becomes sparse, distances become less informative and more data is needed.
detail: Remedies: feature selection, extraction (PCA), regularisation, domain knowledge.
example: k-NN degrades with many irrelevant features.
mistakes: Adding features always improves models.

q: Explain split–apply–combine.
short: Group rows by a key, apply an aggregate per group, combine the results into one table.
detail: pandas: df.groupby('color')['value'].mean(). Aggregation reduces data, changes scale and stabilises variation.
follow: What aggregates suit counts vs rates?
mistakes: Averaging averages with different group sizes.

q: Build a leakage-free preprocessing pipeline for mixed data.
short: Use a ColumnTransformer with imputer+scaler for numeric and imputer+one-hot for categorical, inside a Pipeline with the model.
detail:
prep = ColumnTransformer([
  ('num', make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy='median'), StandardScaler()), num_cols),
  ('cat', make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy='most_frequent'), OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown='ignore')), cat_cols)])
model = make_pipeline(prep, LogisticRegression())
follow: How do you add feature selection?
mistakes: Preprocessing outside the CV loop.

q: Your model works offline but fails on new categories in production. Fix?
short: Handle unknown categories (handle_unknown='ignore' or an 'other' bucket), monitor category drift and retrain.
detail: Also group rare categories during training so the model has seen an 'other' level.
mistakes: Crashing the service on an unseen value.

q: What does 'representative sample' mean and why can a big sample still be biased?
short: It mirrors the population's relevant properties; a flawed sampling process produces bias regardless of size.
detail: Increase size to reduce sampling noise; fix the process (random, stratified) to reduce bias.
example: Phone survey missing people without phones.
follow: Give a sampling-bias example in ML data.
mistakes: Assuming more data fixes bias.

q: Explain MCAR, MAR and MNAR and their effect on imputation.
short: Missing completely at random, at random given observed data, or not at random (depends on the missing value). Simple imputation is unbiased only under MCAR.
detail: MAR can be handled with model-based or multiple imputation using observed variables; MNAR needs domain modelling or indicators.
example: High earners skipping the income question (MNAR).
mistakes: Treating all missingness as random.

q: Why can quartile values differ between tools?
short: There are several percentile definitions (e.g. (n+1)p positions vs linear interpolation on n−1).
detail: The slide's (n+1) rule gives Q3 = 14.75 for the exercise; NumPy's default gives 14.25. Fences shift slightly; conclusions are usually stable.
mistakes: Comparing results across tools without stating the method.

q: When is label encoding acceptable for nominal features?
short: With tree-based models, which split on thresholds and can isolate categories, and for high-cardinality features where one-hot is too large.
detail: Linear and distance models misread integer codes as magnitudes. Target encoding is another option but must be cross-fitted to avoid leakage.
mistakes: Using it with k-NN.

q: Standardising a heavy-tailed feature still hurts your linear model. What next?
short: Transform the shape: log or Box-Cox/Yeo-Johnson, quantile transform, or clip/winsorise; then standardise.
detail: Standardisation is affine and keeps skew. Robust scaling (median/IQR) reduces outlier influence.
mistakes: Expecting z-scores to fix skew.

q: How does SMOTE work and what are its risks?
short: Creates synthetic minority points by interpolating between a minority point and its minority neighbours.
detail: Risks: generating points in majority regions (noise), leakage if applied before splitting, unrealistic samples for categorical data.
mistakes: Applying SMOTE to the test set.

q: PCA as feature extraction: what does it optimise?
short: It finds orthogonal directions of maximum variance; projecting onto the top k keeps most variance.
detail: Eigenvectors of the covariance matrix (or SVD of centred data). Requires scaling when units differ. Unsupervised: may discard label-relevant low-variance directions.
mistakes: Running PCA on unscaled mixed-unit features.

q: Filter vs wrapper vs embedded feature selection?
short: Filters score features independently (correlation, mutual information); wrappers search subsets with a model; embedded methods select during training (Lasso, tree importance).
detail: Filters are fast but ignore interactions; wrappers are expensive and overfit; embedded balance both.
follow: How to avoid selection bias in CV?
mistakes: Selecting features on the full data before CV.

q: Duplicates with conflicting labels appear in your training data. What do you do?
short: Investigate the source; deduplicate by key; resolve conflicts by business rules, majority vote or removal; measure label noise.
detail: Conflicting duplicates (same person, different marital status) indicate entity-resolution or labelling issues that cap achievable accuracy.
mistakes: Keeping duplicates across train and test.

q: Is binning a good idea for continuous features?
short: Sometimes: it adds robustness to outliers and lets linear models capture non-linear effects, but it loses information and adds boundary artefacts.
detail: Prefer splines or tree models when you want non-linearity; bin for interpretability or when algorithms need discrete inputs.
follow: How does binning interact with regularisation?
mistakes: Binning with test-derived edges.

q: Why must every fitted preprocessing step live inside cross-validation?
short: Because its learned statistics carry information about validation folds; fitting outside leaks it and inflates scores.
detail: Pipelines refit imputers, scalers, encoders and selectors on each training fold.
example: Feature selection on all data inflating accuracy.
follow: How large can leakage effects be?
mistakes: Thinking scaling leakage is negligible in every case.
